title: Operator is not a continuation of O3 — it is reasoning's first hand reaching into the physical world
dek: OpenAI tried a Web Agent in 2016, failed, and laid off twenty or thirty people; what was missing was a foundation model. Ten years later, Operator brings together the foundation model, human data and reinforcement learning, and only then does reasoning move from abstract text toward visual interaction.
why: Wu Yi is a former OpenAI researcher and assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences. He breaks down Operator's technical essentials, agent levels and startup opportunities from a reinforcement learning perspective, with high information density — suited to listeners who want to understand the agent technology roadmap.
who: Engineers, founders and investors who want to understand the agent technology roadmap and Operator's positioning, especially those working on reinforcement learning, multimodality or agent products.
skip: The wrap-up and subscription read after 1:11:21 can be skipped.

points.h: Operator is closed-loop control; O1 is open-loop
points.body: Wu Yi defines Operator's place on the AGI roadmap as ‘a general-purpose change’: O1 and O3 are transformations that think on a focused problem, but there is no environment interaction in between, and no multimodality. Operator fills in both — it can see an observation, take one action, then see a new observation, doing many rounds of interaction in a row, forming a closed-loop control system. A traditional large model is open-loop: give it an instruction and it outputs directly, with no feedback wanted; Operator, after outputting, actively calls out and expects the next feedback, then thinks its next step based on that feedback. This ‘horizontal axis’ of general capability is something you must have on the way to a general agent.

points.h: Operator's chain of thought is short; backtracking happens on actions
points.body: Wu Yi does not think Operator is a simple continuation of O1 and O3. Observing the chain of thought Operator released, he finds it relatively short, and backtracking mainly appears on actions — for example, it clicks a webpage and it doesn't open for a long time, so it clicks back. O1 and O3's chains of thought are very, very long, with lots of backtracking. So he leans toward thinking Operator is not as extreme a model as O3, more like ‘a multimodal closed-loop O1, an Agent O1 version’, or possibly a spot a bit more O1. It moves wider in breadth rather than to the extreme in depth, so there is still room.

points.h: Replicating Operator takes three things; China is not that far off
points.body: Wu Yi breaks Operator's technical essentials into three: a good native multimodal foundation model, high-quality human data and tasks, and an efficient large-scale reinforcement learning system that supports agents. The third is the most troublesome, because in an agent environment the model spits out a few hundred tokens and then has to click on the screen; you need a computer sitting there waiting for the AI to click, doing simulation, and how to interact efficiently at the scale of several thousand or ten thousand cards is a research problem. But he judges that domestic teams catching up to Operator is not as hard as catching up to GPT or Sora: the route is clear, much of the infrastructure is already there, it is a half there state. The problem is you don't know how much OpenAI has underwater.

points.h: OpenAI's first big project was a Web Agent, and it failed
points.body: Wu Yi goes back to 2016: the first big project OpenAI did after being founded was a Web Agent, a general visual agent clicking on webpages. At the time they only had reinforcement learning, no foundation model, and nobody even went to find data annotation, there wasn't even transmission; they used a big LSTM called Covnet to click webpages, clicking with reinforcement learning, and then it failed, and they laid off that team, laid off twenty or thirty people. Wu Yi tells this story to students in his deep learning class, saying the missing recipe at the time was the foundation model — reinforcement learning alone won't do, and a good foundation model alone won't quite do either, you need the two together. Ten years later they got it done.

points.h: Level three to four is a very big change, not just two or three years
points.body: Wu Yi unpacks OpenAI's five-level classification: a chatbot is reactive, you say a line and I say a line; reasoning is thinking in your head for ten seconds before speaking, with reasoning and planning; an agent then adds an external world, it is a three-party process, the AI's scope gets bigger. But levels one to three are all instruction following or instruction execution: give an instruction, complete it, and you can verify right or wrong. Innovation is different — you can only give something directional, right and wrong have no meaning, what you want is something better than the original knowledge system. Wu Yi thinks three to four is a very big change, possibly not achievable in just two or three years. And which of four and five comes first is not certain; organizations may form passively — in the future every piece of software will carry an agent, and interactions will exist between them.

points.h: Multi-agent interaction will not appear any time soon
points.body: Wu Yi's view is that for the time being, situations where multiple agents interact will not appear. Because if the goal is to complete a task, a sufficiently general large model can do everything itself — O1 and O3 have already proven that as long as reinforcement learning training is in place and context and memory are super long, ten thousand tokens is no problem, and the reasoning process is still clear. Multi-agent interaction will definitely happen when a task involves an AI being passively triggered in the middle, for example in the future every website's entrance is also an agent, or you have the AI look something up on Doubao (豆包) or ChatGPT. But for the time being most human-computer interaction interfaces are still graphical interfaces, still designed for people, so the next year or two is still a single-agent state.

points.h: Operator's user data is far more valuable than a chatbot's
points.body: Wu Yi agrees with Guangmi that a chatbot cannot help improve intelligence — small talk has no intelligence, and the dialogue form by default mostly does not produce a deliberative process. But Operator is different: when do you need a person to help you click webpages? Usually you have a purpose, like calculating personal income tax or booking a complex itinerary; the query distribution is very different from a chatbot's, relatively heavy. So if you can collect such user feedback and final completion signals, it helps improve the model's general capability. OpenAI has an option not to submit your user scripts; Wu Yi says this kind of instruction carrying a complex task, plus the judgment data of whether it was completed, is very suitable for reinforcement learning training, and if a hard problem is found, reinforcement learning training needs very little data.

points.h: Operator is a signal, not intelligence in the physical world
points.body: Wu Yi has long held a view: intelligence splits into two parts, one is reasoning in the pure text modality, one is reasoning over visual signals, and the two are not quite the same. Operator has not really gone into the physical world now, it is still at the software webpage level, and webpages are mostly designed for people to browse, with a relatively strong textual concept. So what it shows is the beginning of a possibility; it has not truly dragged the possibility out. It expanded capability, but the intelligence ceiling did not rise — pure logical reasoning is not stronger than O3, and physical-world reasoning has not arrived either. Wu Yi uses a pointer as a metaphor: originally it was a 90-degree pointer always going north, now it has expanded a bit to the right from 90 degrees, maybe to 80 degrees, and you don't know where it will go.

quotes.text: It's that foundation model. Without a good foundation model, reinforcement learning alone won't do. But look, a good foundation model alone won't quite do either, right? You still have to add reinforcement learning, the two together.

But innovation is different. Innovation is actually that you can only give something directional. For example, we know students, we know PhD students writing papers — you actually can't say whether this thing is right or wrong, because right and wrong have no meaning anymore, because if it's innovation, it's certainly right.
So if through that kind of massive user feedback it can't improve intelligence, it can only improve the product's comfort, so that's fine. But I think Operator is relatively a little different.
It only shows the beginning of this possibility; it has not truly dragged this possibility out.
